title: Why Can't Anyone Agree on the Day Pompeii Disappeared? The Month Nobody Can Prove
parts: Why can't anyone agree on the day Pompeii disappeared?
The textbooks say Vesuvius began burying the city on August twenty-fourth, seventy-nine.
That is what the guidebooks say.
But a scribble in charcoal, found in twenty eighteen, gives a date in October.
About two months apart.
Fruit, wool, braziers, even a coin, all seem to vote.
And nobody has seen the original letter behind the date.
So which month is right?
Let's follow the clues.
We will mark each one: documented, disputed, or myth.
Some will surprise you.
Some will not survive the checking.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, why does it matter?
Kristina Killgrove is a scientist who studies ancient Romans.
She points out that many diseases have seasonal peaks.
She says two months matter for studying who lived there.
Pompeii is not just a famous ruin.
It is a time capsule, and a time capsule needs a date.
So here is where the trail starts.
With a letter.
The writer is Pliny the Younger.
He wrote to his friend Tacitus, a historian.
Tacitus had asked how Pliny's uncle died.
Pliny answers in a long letter.
In it, he describes a cloud above the mountain.
It looked like a tree, he says, and a pine tree most of all.
Then comes the date.
He writes it the Roman way.
The Latin says: the ninth day before the Kalends of September.
The Kalends was the first day of a Roman month.
Romans counted backwards from it, including the first day itself.
So the ninth day before September first is August twenty-fourth.
Pliny wrote it around the year one hundred and eight, decades later.
It is the main eyewitness account we have.
So the famous date rests on one man's letter.
And that letter has a problem.
Nobody has Pliny's original.
What survives are medieval copies of copies.
The oldest copies, from the ninth century, point to August.
But a fifteenth-century copy in Paris leaves the month out.
A printed edition from fourteen seventy-four says November.
In seventeen ninety-seven, another editor suggested late November.
Some scholars see in the November reading a trace of October twenty-fourth.
That is a debate about handwriting, not about volcanoes.
Gabriel Zuchtriegel directs the Pompeii archaeological park.
He says August is the only date in the manuscripts.
But he adds that this does not prove it.
So the letter alone cannot settle it.
Now let's leave the letter and walk the streets.
Archaeologists found dried figs, walnuts, and chestnuts.
They also found pomegranates.
Those fruits sound like autumn.
Some wine jars were already sealed.
They found braziers, bowls for hot coals.
And they found traces of woollen clothing.
That is the autumn case.
But every clue has a plain answer.
Fleeing people may have put on warm clothes against the ash.
Braziers also cooked food.
One archaeologist argues that for the Romans, August was already autumn.
So the fruit could be ripe.
An expert in ancient plants says the grape harvest apparently had not begun.
Cassius Dio, writing later, gives no day.
In one translation, he puts it at the very end of summer.
His Greek word can mean late summer, or autumn.
Even the wording is disputed.
Researchers in Valencia, in a study presented at a conference, looked at fourteen plaster casts.
In only four could the garment type be confirmed: heavy wool.
Now, a coin.
A silver denarius from Pompeii shows the emperor Titus.
Emperors collected titles over time.
One of them was imperator, an acclamation that was counted.
In two thousand six, the coin was read as showing the fifteenth acclamation.
But two documents from early September list only the fourteenth.
If both are right, the coin must come later.
Yet British coin experts in twenty thirteen saw no proof of that number.
Then, in October twenty eighteen, came the scribble.
In a house reported as a building site, someone found a charcoal inscription.
It reads, in Roman style, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.
By the same counting, that is October seventeenth.
There is no year.
The park's director then, Massimo Osanna, called it a joking phrase.
He imagined a good-tempered worker writing on a wall, and called it extraordinary evidence of a secure date.
The Ministry of Culture reasoned that charcoal is fragile.
So, they argued, it was most likely written in October of seventy-nine.
That made October the favored date for years.
Here is our reading.
It shows someone wrote that day on that wall.
It cannot tell us the year.
So, can charcoal last ten months?
The park decided to test it.
On October seventeenth, twenty twenty-three, they wrote on the same wall, under a rain cover.
They reportedly used oak charcoal.
Same date, plus the year and the words experimental archaeology.
They photographed it every month.
The park reports it was essentially unaltered on August twenty-fourth, twenty twenty-four.
Still perfectly legible.
Zuchtriegel co-authored the report, published in December twenty twenty-four.
His line: right now, we cannot exclude August twenty-fourth.
It does not prove August. It weakens one argument against it.
Now, an animal.
In twenty twenty-two, the park announced a Hermann's tortoise.
She was in a shop near the Stabian Baths, with one egg.
But the park says rubble covered her during rebuilding, before the eruption.
A tortoise that died before the eruption cannot date it.
So we do not count her vote.
Then there are the volcanologists.
A team reviewed the whole eruption again.
Their press release leans toward autumn.
It calls October twenty-fourth to twenty-fifth the most accredited date.
They cite the scribble, the fruit, and the heavy clothes.
Same clues we just heard.
A strong voice, but not the final word.
Two camps, same evidence.
Before we count the votes, one more story about Pompeii.
It is about stories we told ourselves.
You may know the plaster casts of Pompeii.
They are made by pouring plaster into hollows in the hardened ash.
For generations, people told family stories about some of them.
A mother with her child.
Two sisters, hugging.
In twenty twenty-four, a team from Florence, Harvard, and the Max Planck Institute tested that.
They sampled fourteen of eighty-six casts then under restoration.
Five gave usable genome-wide data.
The adult wearing a golden bracelet, long read as a mother, was a man.
He was not related to the child beside him.
In the embracing pair, thought to be sisters, one was male.
The paper says the casts were considerably manipulated, and likely restored creatively.
Co-author Caramelli suggests restorers may have changed poses to fit a story.
These two family stories do not hold up.
Our reading: in both cases, the story ran ahead of the evidence.
Now back to the date.
Let's count the clues.
The oldest copies of Pliny's letter say August. That is documented.
Other copies say other months. Also documented.
Fruit, wool, braziers, jars: found, yes. What they prove is disputed.
The coin of Titus is disputed.
The scribble is documented. The year is disputed.
The tortoise does not count. The volcanologists' date is disputed.
The idea that one scribble settles it is a myth.
Those two family stories are myths too.
So the month stays an open question.
Here are the open hypotheses.
One: Pliny's letter says August, and the autumn clues have plain answers.
Two: the date was October, and the letter was copied wrongly.
Three: we still lack the document that would settle it.
Our reading: each clue has a simple alternative.
So the winner will need a month and a year, together.
Maybe a dated document, found in a sealed layer.
Our reading: until then, the textbook date is a tradition, not a proof.
And that is the thing about famous dates.
We repeat them so often that we forget to check.
Which famous date have you repeated for years, and never checked?
